sections.title: Reflections on facilitating the Olot Children's Council 2025-2026

children.text: <cite> What happens when we listen to children's voices and include them in political participation?</cite>

Children look at the world with alert, attentive eyes. Curious, they ask why the reality they live in is the way it is, and it has become clear that they are citizens with many ideas, often original and creative ones.

Children inhabit the towns and villages where they live. They move through them every day, often on foot, by scooter or by bike, to get to and from school, take part in after-school activities and enjoy public spaces. Although we adults tend to think that children play in the street less than they used to, boys and girls fill squares and parks every afternoon, and these remain places for meeting and playing. They take part in cultural, festive and folk-culture activities (perhaps even more than many adults) and enjoy the natural surroundings.

Perhaps having lived only a few years, and living in the present with an intensity that many of us adults have lost, allows them to truly inhabit and experience the place where they live in a unique way.
And it is this inhabiting that gives them the right, the legitimacy and the full capacity to take part in the political and democratic life of the place where they live as well.
It is not just about listening to children because they are the future, but because they are already part of the city's present. They live it, move through it, suffer it, enjoy it and imagine it.
The first condition for participating is wanting to do so, and running the Children's Council has made it clear to us that girls and boys are eager to.

With this in mind, we wanted to offer a space for real participation for the children of Olot, one that could capture this everyday perspective and help them turn it into a collective contribution to improving and transforming the city.

The 2025-2026 Children's Council involved seven schools in the town of Olot, with thirteen Year 5 primary groups (ages 10-11) and around three hundred pupils, twenty-six of whom acted as representatives of their schools. During the process, three sessions were held with each group, thirty-nine sessions in total, plus three sessions with the representatives. The work focused on the environment, public space and leisure, culture and community, and through dialogue and prioritisation thirteen concrete proposals were developed and presented at the Extraordinary Plenary Session of Olot Town Council on 4 June.

Throughout the sessions, both in the classrooms and with the representatives from each school, we were able to open up a space for sensitivity, presentation, debate and reflection. At all times we tried to put the focus on the voices and ideas of the children, who felt this opportunity to improve their surroundings. Building on this trust, we were able to go deeper into the issues that concern them.

It has been interesting to accompany them on the journey of looking for the deepest roots of problems, and to see how quickly they realised that many of the issues we can observe in our town (such as litter in the streets or pollution in the river) have to do with behaviours, relationships and deeper structures. For this reason, to remedy them, we need to design solutions aimed at these less superficial, underlying layers rather than at what is visible at first sight.

However, during the process we came across some concerns. At first, the children's initial ideas and proposals for tackling the problems and needs they identified were very punitive, prohibitive and coercive: video surveillance, fines… Even so, when they were asked to reflect on what moved and motivated them to do things, they realised that they do not like punishment and that it makes them feel frustrated, sad and uneasy. Constructive, positive proposals, on the other hand, are what generate motivation, hope and the desire to do things.

We have also seen how issues such as poverty, theft, housing, the need for safe spaces and the environment became focal points for debate, for exchanging ideas and, at times, for surprise. At the same time, they allowed us to detect discourses that often do not originate with the children themselves, but in an increasingly polarised social context.

We are concerned that this discourse is being reproduced by children. Perhaps it has always been this way, just as childhood has always been a time when everything is possible and education has the capacity to shape generations who believe in and act on values of cooperation, personal agency and critical thinking. This experience has shown us the responsibility we have to foster dialogue, listening and joy beyond fear.

For us, as young people from Olot and the Garrotxa connected to Núria Social, this has been a unique opportunity offered to us by Pegàs de Foc. It has allowed us to develop our skills in facilitating processes of democratic participation and community development, and to get involved, in a supporting role, in improving and transforming the place where we live, through active listening and a sensitivity to including every voice.

The challenge from now on is to make sure this process does not end here. The proposals presented by the children need clear, honest and understandable feedback: which ones can go ahead, which will take more time, which depend on other actors and which, perhaps, will not be possible as they were formulated. Without this feedback, there is a risk that participation is reduced to a symbolic exercise. When children can see that what they have thought about, debated and proposed has real consequences, however, the process becomes a positive experience of collective democratic participation that they will be able to repeat and demand in the future.

This is also a lesson for adults. Listening to children does not just mean giving them the floor on specific occasions, but incorporating their perspective into the way we think about the city, its neighbourhoods, public spaces, culture, leisure and living together. Democratic participation is learnt by practising it, and that is why we need to create stable, well-cared-for and recognised spaces where children can express themselves, deliberate and have an influence.

For this reason, we believe the Children's Council should continue as a participatory body and be consolidated beyond a one-off educational experience. It would also be interesting to explore how to scale this space up to a wider territorial level and how to link it with other existing participatory spaces, such as village councils or other community bodies.

If we want a more vibrant, closer and more inclusive democracy, we must accept that children's voices are not just an add-on, but an essential part of the collective conversation about the present and future of the place where we live.
